mainTopic: The סדר: dipping and washing, eating מצה and מרור, the table, and לחם עוני
overview: This amud continues the rules of dipping at the סדר. The גמרא first tries to prove from the washing of hands that the lettuce must be pushed fully into the חרוסת to kill the קפא, but rejects the proof: perhaps the smell is enough, and we wash only in case someone submerges it. רב פפא warns not to leave the מרור in the חרוסת too long, so its bitter taste is not lost. רבנא עוקבא teaches that one washes again for the second dipping. The רבנן and רב פפא argue whether this refers to an ordinary meal or to פסח night. The answer is that on פסח night the long הגדה and הלל may distract a person, so he washes again. רבא then teaches that swallowing מצה counts but swallowing מרור does not. Next comes the arrangement of the סדר table, where the הלכה follows רב הונא, and the removal of the table so the children will ask, as in the story of young אביי. The amud ends with שמואל's reading of לחם עוני, and a second reading that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Lettuce must be submerged in the חרוסת
steps.stepSummary: The lettuce used for מרור must be pushed into the חרוסת to neutralize a harmful substance called קפא.
steps.simpleTranslation: One must submerge it (the lettuce) in the חרוסת, because of the קפא (a harmful substance in the lettuce).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states a rule that continues from the discussion on the previous amud: the lettuce for מרור has to be put fully into the חרוסת. The reason is to kill a harmful substance in it called קפא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lettuce (חסא) was thought to contain something harmful, a kind of poison or bitter 'worm'. The sharp חרוסת neutralizes it. So the חרוסת here has a health purpose, not only a taste or symbolic one.

keyTerms.meaning: to submerge it / push it fully in
the paste of fruits and spices that the מרור is dipped into
a harmful substance (poison) found in lettuce

phrases.english: one must submerge it in the charoses,
phrases.notes: 'It' refers to the lettuce used for מרור.

phrases.english: because of the 'kappa' (harmful substance).
phrases.notes: רש"י explains it's a kind of poison in the lettuce that the חרוסת kills.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion about washing hands before dipping, and draws a practical rule from it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The lettuce must be fully submerged in the חרוסת to neutralize the קפא.

steps.title: Proof from the requirement to wash hands
steps.stepSummary: If the lettuce did not need to be submerged, there would be no reason to wash hands, because the hands would never touch the חרוסת.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you thought that one need not submerge it, why would I need washing of hands? He did not touch it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a proof for the rule in step 1. It points to the requirement to wash hands before dipping.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We wash hands before dipping food in a liquid so our hands do not make the liquid טמא. If you only touched the tip of the lettuce to the חרוסת, your fingers would never reach the liquid, and washing would be pointless. So the fact that we wash shows that the lettuce is pushed deep in, and the fingers may touch the חרוסת.

keyTerms.meaning: for if it would enter your mind (if you thought)

phrases.english: for if it would enter your mind
phrases.notes: This phrase kicks off a proof: 'if you thought otherwise, look what would happen.'

phrases.english: that one need not submerge it —
why do I need washing of hands?
he did not touch it!
phrases.notes: His hands never reach the liquid, so they cannot make it impure.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ לָא צְרִיךְ לְשַׁקּוֹעֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rule of step 1.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that the lettuce must be fully submerged in the חרוסת.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The established requirement of נטילת ידים before dipping, which only makes sense if the hands might touch the liquid.

steps.title: Maybe the smell alone kills the poison
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof: maybe submerging is not needed at all, because the smell of the חרוסת is enough to kill the קפא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps I can really tell you: one need not submerge it, and the קפא dies from the smell.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. It suggests that the lettuce does not need to go fully into the חרוסת, because the smell of the חרוסת is enough to neutralize the קפא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This removes the health reason for submerging. If the smell does the job, a light dip is enough. That reopens the question from step 2: why wash hands? The next step asks this directly.

keyTerms.meaning: really, I can tell you (the opposite)

phrases.english: But perhaps I can really tell you:
one need not submerge it,
and the kappa dies from the smell.
phrases.notes: The smell of the חרוסת alone neutralizes the harmful substance.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 2 by offering another way the קפא is neutralized.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof that submerging is required by offering a possible alternative. It does not reject the washing requirement itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed that only submerging can neutralize the קפא. But the smell might be enough.

steps.title: Then why wash hands?
steps.stepSummary: If submerging is not needed, the original question returns: why wash hands at all?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then why do I need washing of hands?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rejection in step 3. If you do not have to submerge the lettuce, what is the point of washing hands?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same question from step 2, now aimed at the new view. If the hands never touch the חרוסת, washing seems unnecessary.

phrases.english: But then why do I need washing of hands —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view of step 3 that submerging is not needed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without submerging, the hands never touch the liquid. So the washing requirement would have no purpose.

steps.title: We wash in case someone submerges it
steps.stepSummary: Washing is required because a person might choose to submerge the lettuce anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps he will submerge it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Even if submerging is not required, some people might do it, so we require washing for everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Washing is a precaution, not a sign that submerging is required. Because of this, the proof in step 2 falls apart. The washing rule fits both views.
steps.whatToRemember: The proof that lettuce must be submerged is rejected. Washing could just be a precaution in case someone does submerge it, and perhaps the smell of the חרוסת is enough to kill the קפא.

phrases.english: Perhaps he will submerge it.
phrases.notes: So washing is required as a precaution.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4 and defends step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Precautionary reasoning: the rule covers a possible case, not the required case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Washing hands proves the lettuce must be submerged.
steps.terutzMaskana: Washing can be explained as a safeguard in case someone submerges it. So the washing requirement no longer proves that submerging is required.

steps.title: Do not leave the מרור in the חרוסת too long
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rules that the מרור should not stay in the חרוסת long, because the sweetness may cancel its bitter taste.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב פפא said: A person should not leave מרור in the חרוסת for long, lest the sweetness of the spices cancel its bitterness. We need the taste of מרור, and it would be missing.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a new rule about the חרוסת. Dip the מרור and take it out quickly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole point of מרור is its bitter taste. If it soaks in sweet חרוסת, the bitterness can be cancelled, and the מצוה would be missing. So the dip should be short.

keyTerms.meaning: should not leave it (for a long time)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical סדר rule: dip the מרור briefly. It shows that the bitter taste is essential to the מצוה.

phrases.english: And Rav Pappa said:
a person should not leave maror in the charoses for long,
lest because of the sweetness of the spices
it cancels its bitterness,
and we require the taste of maror, and it is not there.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לָא נִישַׁהֵי אִינִישׁ מָרוֹר בַּחֲרוֹסֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, related rule about dipping מרור in חרוסת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מרור should not stay in the חרוסת for long, so its bitter taste is not cancelled.

steps.title: Wash again for the second dipping
steps.stepSummary: רבנא עוקבא teaches publicly that someone who washed for the first dipping must wash again for the second dipping.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא appointed רבנא עוקבא to teach, and he taught: If one washed his hands for the first dipping, he washes his hands for the second dipping.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching is introduced: washing for the first dipping does not cover the second. This sets up the argument in the next steps about what situation it refers to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule says each dipping needs its own washing. It does not say whether it means פסח night (כרפס and then מרור) or any meal. That unclear point is what the רבנן and רב פפא will argue about.

phrases.aramaic: אַדְבְּרֵיהּ רַב חִסְדָּא לְרַבָּנָא עוּקְבָא, וּדְרַשׁ:
phrases.english: Rav Chisda appointed Rabbana Ukva, and he taught:
if he washed his hands for the first dipping —
he washes his hands for the second dipping.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְבְּרֵיהּ רַב חִסְדָּא לְרַבָּנָא עוּקְבָא, וּדְרַשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a new teaching about washing for dipping.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who washed for the first dipping must wash again for the second dipping.

steps.title: The רבנן say it refers to an ordinary meal
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן tell רב פפא that this teaching was said about meals in general, not about פסח night.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן said this before רב פפא: This was stated about the general case (not about פסח).
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן offer their reading of רבנא עוקבא's teaching: it refers to any meal during the year. Their reason comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is about scope: where does the rule apply? The רבנן limit it to everyday meals and leave פסח night out.

keyTerms.meaning: the Rabbis said it before him

phrases.english: The Rabbis said it before Rav Pappa:
This was stated about the general case.
phrases.notes: Meaning any meal during the year, not the סדר.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמְרוּהָ רַבָּנַן קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב פָּפָּא: הָא בְּעָלְמָא אִיתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the scope of the teaching in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The teaching of step 7 applies to ordinary meals, not to פסח night.

steps.title: On פסח one already guards his hands
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן argue that on פסח night a second washing is pointless, because he already washed and knows another dipping is coming.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you thought it was stated here (about פסח), why do I need washing of hands twice? He already washed his hands once!
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן prove their reading. On פסח night, washing twice makes no sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At the סדר, a person knows from the start that a second dipping (מרור) will follow the first (כרפס). So he will guard his hands from becoming טמא, and his first washing still holds. A second washing only makes sense in an ordinary meal, where he did not plan to dip again and was not careful.

phrases.english: For if you thought it was stated here,

phrases.aramaic: לְמָה לִי נְטִילַת יָדַיִם תְּרֵי זִימְנֵי?
phrases.english: why do I need washing of hands two times?

phrases.aramaic: הָא מְשָׁא לֵיהּ יְדֵיהּ חֲדָא זִימְנָא!
phrases.english: he already washed his hands once!
phrases.notes: Knowing another dipping is coming, he would guard his hands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves the reading of the רבנן in step 8.
steps.raayaObject: That the teaching refers to ordinary meals.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Logic: on פסח night the first washing is still valid, because he guards his hands, knowing another dipping is coming.

steps.title: רב פפא says the opposite
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rejects the רבנן and says the teaching was said specifically about פסח night.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to them: On the contrary, it was stated here (about פסח).
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא turns the argument around. The teaching is about פסח night, not ordinary meals. His proof comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אדרבה signals a full reversal, not just a weak doubt. רב פפא argues that the very case the רבנן excluded is the one the teaching is about.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to them:
On the contrary, it was stated here.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב פָּפָּא: אַדְּרַבָּה, הָכָא אִיתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reading of the רבנן in steps 8-9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the teaching applies to ordinary meals.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The רבנן ignored that a 'second dipping' is not a normal part of an ordinary meal (explained in the next step).

steps.title: Only פסח night has two dippings
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא proves his view: in an ordinary meal there are not two dippings, so a teaching about a 'second dipping' must mean פסח night.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you thought it was stated about the general case, why would I need two dippings?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives his proof. Normally people do not dip twice in a meal, so the case of a 'second dipping' must be the סדר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only on פסח night does the מצוה require two dippings: כרפס and then מרור. A teaching that speaks about a 'second dipping' fits that night best. So רב פפא reads the teaching as being about the סדר, even though the hands were already washed once.
steps.whatToRemember: רבנא עוקבא taught: wash for the first dipping and again for the second. The רבנן say this means ordinary meals, since on פסח he guards his hands after the first washing. רב פפא says it means פסח night, since only then are there two dippings.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two arguments. The רבנן ask, 'Why wash twice?' and argue from the washing. רב פפא asks, 'Why dip twice?' and argues from the dippings. Each side uses a different detail of the same teaching.

phrases.english: For if you thought it was stated about the general case,
why do I need two dippings?
phrases.notes: Ordinarily a person dips only once in a meal.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ בְּעָלְמָא אִיתְּמַר, לְמָה לִי תְּרֵי טִיבּוּלֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב פפא's reversal in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: That the teaching of רבנא עוקבא refers to פסח night.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Logic: two dippings are found only at the סדר, not at an ordinary meal.

steps.title: If it was said about פסח night, why wash twice?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב פפא: if the teaching is about פסח night, why would anyone need to wash a second time after already washing once?
steps.simpleTranslation: But what will you say, that it was said here, about פסח night? Why do I need to wash hands two times? He already washed his hands once!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב פפא's view that the teaching was said about פסח night. It asks why a second washing would be needed when he already washed once.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This revives the רבנן's original argument from step 9. If the hands are already clean from the first washing, a second washing looks pointless. רב פפא's reading now needs a reason for the second washing.

keyTerms.meaning: But what then? (a formula that challenges the alternative view)

phrases.english: Rather, what? It was stated here (about Passover night)?

phrases.aramaic: נְטִילַת יָדַיִם תְּרֵי זִימְנֵי לְמָה לִי?
phrases.english: Why do I need washing of hands two times?

phrases.aramaic: הָא מְשָׁא לֵיהּ יְדֵיהּ חֲדָא זִימְנָא!
phrases.english: He already washed his hands one time!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's conclusion from step 11 by bringing back the logic of the רבנן in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's claim that רבנא עוקבא's teaching was said about פסח night.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: On פסח night he already washed for the first dipping, so the second washing seems to have no purpose.

steps.title: He may lose focus during the הגדה and touch something
steps.stepSummary: The answer: between the two dippings he says the הגדה and הלל, so he may stop paying attention and touch something impure. That is why he washes again.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: Since he needs to say the הגדה and הלל, maybe he will take his mind off his hands and touch something.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The long break for the הגדה and הלל means his hands may have become impure without his noticing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first washing does not automatically last all night. Watching over clean hands requires paying attention, and a long recitation makes it likely he stopped paying attention. So the second washing is real and needed, and רב פפא's reading holds.

keyTerms.meaning: Taking one's mind off something; losing focus (the idea behind אַסּוֹחֵי אַסְּחֵיהּ לְדַעְתֵּיהּ)

steps.whatToRemember: On פסח night we wash before the first dipping and again before the second dipping (the מרור). The second washing is needed because the long הגדה and הלל may cause us to lose focus on keeping our hands clean.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the two washings at the סדר, ורחץ and רחצה.

phrases.english: They say: Since he needs
to recite the Haggadah and Hallel,
perhaps he will divert his mind (from guarding his hands)
and touch (something impure).

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: כֵּיוָן דְּבָעֵי לְמֵימַר אַגָּדְתָּא וְהַלֵּילָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12 and defends רב פפא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a new reason that explains the second washing.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One washing is enough because the hands are still clean.
steps.terutzMaskana: The long break for the הגדה and הלל causes loss of focus, so a second washing is needed.

steps.title: Swallowing works for מצה but not for מרור
steps.stepSummary: רבא teaches that swallowing מצה without chewing counts, but swallowing מרור without chewing does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If he swallowed מצה, he fulfilled his obligation. If he swallowed מרור, he did not fulfill his obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new teaching from רבא about how מצה and מרור must be eaten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מצה only needs to be eaten, and swallowing is a form of eating. מרור is meant to make you taste bitterness, so swallowing it whole without tasting misses the point.

keyTerms.meaning: He did not fulfill his obligation

phrases.english: Rava said: If he swallowed matza, he fulfilled his obligation;
if he swallowed bitter herbs, he did not fulfill his obligation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. It moves from washing hands to how the סדר foods are eaten.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Swallowing מצה counts, but swallowing מרור does not, because the bitter taste is required.

steps.title: Swallowing מצה and מרור together, or wrapped in palm fiber
steps.stepSummary: רבא continues: swallowing both together counts for מצה but not מרור. If they are wrapped in palm fiber and swallowed, it does not even count for מצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he swallowed מצה and מרור together, he fulfilled the obligation of מצה but not of מרור. If he wrapped them in palm fiber and swallowed them, he did not fulfill even the obligation of מצה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא applies his rule to two harder cases: eating both together, and eating them wrapped in palm fiber.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Together, each food keeps its own rule: the מצה counts as swallowed and the מרור fails as before. When wrapped in a palm net, the מצה never touches the mouth, so the act is not called eating at all.

keyTerms.meaning: The obligation of (literally: the hands of)

steps.confusionAlert: The palm-fiber case does not fail because of mixing with מרור. It fails because the מצה never touches the mouth, so it is not considered eating.

phrases.english: If he swallowed matza and bitter herbs together,
he fulfilled the obligation of matza,
but he did not fulfill the obligation of bitter herbs.
If he wrapped them in palm fiber and swallowed them,

phrases.aramaic: אַף יְדֵי מַצָּה נָמֵי לֹא יָצָא.
phrases.english: he did not fulfill even the obligation of matza.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּלַע מַצָּה וּמָרוֹר, יְדֵי מַצָּה — יָצָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבא's teaching from step 14 with harder cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Together, swallowing counts for מצה only. Wrapped in palm fiber, it does not count for either, because there is no contact with the mouth.

steps.title: Each person gets their own מצה, מרור, and חרוסת
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי בר אשי says מצה, מרור, and חרוסת are placed before every participant, and only the leader's table is removed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי בר אשי said: מצה goes before each person, מרור goes before each person, and חרוסת goes before each person. And the table is removed only from in front of the one who says the הגדה.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching about setting the seder table. רב שימי בר אשי says every participant has the foods placed in front of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In those days each diner had a small personal table. Removing the table makes the children ask questions, but רב שימי בר אשי says this is done only for the leader's table, while everyone else keeps their foods.

keyTerms.meaning: A sweet dip for the מרור
The telling of the Exodus story at the seder

phrases.english: Rav Shimi bar Ashi said:
Matza is placed before each and every one,
bitter herbs before each and every one,
and haroset before each and every one.
And the table is not removed
except from before the one who recites the Haggadah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי: מַצָּה לִפְנֵי כׇּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic about how the seder table is arranged.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every participant has מצה, מרור, and חרוסת in front of them, and only the leader's table is removed.

steps.title: רב הונא: the foods are placed only before the leader
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא disagrees and says all these foods are placed only before the person saying the הגדה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא says: All of them are also placed only before the one who says the הגדה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives an opposing view to רב שימי בר אשי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב הונא, only the leader has the מצה, מרור, and חרוסת. When it is time to eat them, he hands portions out to everyone else.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who recites the הגדה (the seder leader)

phrases.english: Rav Huna says: All of them also
are placed only before the one who recites the Haggadah.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא אוֹמֵר: כּוּלְּהוּ נָמֵי לִפְנֵי מִי שֶׁאוֹמֵר הַגָּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב שימי בר אשי in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מצה, מרור, and חרוסת are placed only before the seder leader.

steps.title: The הלכה follows רב הונא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules that the הלכה follows רב הונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the halacha is like רב הונא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the disagreement and rules like רב הונא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seder foods are placed before the leader, who distributes them. This is the basis for the leader's קערה, or seder plate.
steps.whatToRemember: The הלכה follows רב הונא: the סדר foods sit before the person who leads the הגדה, and he gives them out to the others.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the custom that the leader has the main seder plate.

phrases.english: And the halakha is in accordance with Rav Huna.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides between steps 16 and 17.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The halacha follows רב הונא: the seder foods are placed only before the leader of the הגדה.

steps.title: Why is the table removed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind removing the table at the סדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do we remove the table?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the table is removed at the סדר, a practice mentioned just before this. It is setting up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב שימי בר אשי mentioned in step 16 that the table is removed from before the one who says the הגדה. Taking food away before anyone has eaten seems strange, so the גמרא wants to know the purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: table (in that era, a small individual tray-table)

phrases.english: Why do they remove the table?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the table-removal practice mentioned in steps 16 to 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The purpose of removing the table before the meal.

steps.title: So the children notice and ask
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ינאי explains that the table is removed so that children will notice something unusual and ask questions.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ינאי says: so that the children will notice and ask.
steps.whatsHappening: The students of רבי ינאי answer that the table is removed to make children curious enough to ask questions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סדר is designed to get children to ask. Removing food before the meal has even started is so unusual that a child will want to know why. That question opens the way to telling the story of יציאת מצרים.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basic principle behind many unusual סדר customs: they exist to prompt children's questions.

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yannai say:
So that the children will notice and ask.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The table is removed to arouse the children's curiosity so that they ask questions.

steps.title: Young אביי asks why the table is being taken away
steps.stepSummary: A story: אביי, as a child at רבה's table, saw the table being removed and protested that they had not eaten yet.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי was sitting before רבה. He saw that they were lifting the tray away from in front of him. He said to them: We have not eaten yet, and you are already taking the tray away from us?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story in which the young אביי notices the table being removed and asks about it. This sets up רבה's response in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story shows רבי ינאי's reason working in real life. The removal surprised the child, and he asked exactly the kind of question the practice was meant to trigger.
steps.confusionAlert: Here רבה is אביי's uncle, who raised him, and אביי is a young child. Do not mix him up with רבא, a different אמורא who appears in earlier steps.

phrases.english: Abaye was sitting before Rabba,
he saw that they were lifting the tray from before him,
he said to them:
We have not yet eaten,
and they come and remove the tray from before us?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the reason from step 20 playing out in real life.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the tray is being removed before anyone has eaten.

steps.title: רבה: you have exempted us from מה נשתנה
steps.stepSummary: רבה tells אביי that his question already serves the purpose of מה נשתנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said to him: You have exempted us from saying מה נשתנה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers that אביי's question did the job, so they no longer need to say מה נשתנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point of מה נשתנה is for someone to ask about the night's differences. Since אביי asked on his own, the goal was achieved. This shows that the key requirement is a real question, not a fixed script.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Why is this night different', the סדר questions

steps.whatToRemember: The table is removed so children will ask. A child's own question can fulfill the purpose of מה נשתנה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the heart of the הגדה is answering a sincere question.

phrases.english: Rabba said to him:
You have exempted us from saying 'Why is it different.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question and closes the table-removal topic.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A child's spontaneous question replaces the formal מה נשתנה.

steps.title: שמואל: bread over which words are said
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains לחם עוני as bread over which we 'answer' words, meaning we say the הגדה over the מצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: It is written 'לחם עוני', meaning bread over which we answer (say) words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic: שמואל explains the phrase לחם עוני from the פסוק as describing מצה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל reads the word עוני as coming from the root ענה, 'to answer' or 'to speak,' instead of 'poverty.' This teaches that the הגדה should be said over the מצה, while it is in front of us.

keyTerms.meaning: bread of affliction, a name for מצה (דברים טז:ג)
that we answer or recite over it

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for keeping the מצה uncovered and present while saying the הגדה.

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
'Bread of affliction (lechem oni)' is written,
bread over which one answers words.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: how the פסוק describes מצה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: לחם עוני means bread over which the הגדה is recited.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports שמואל
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches the same explanation: לחם עוני is bread over which many words are said.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way: 'לחם עוני' is bread over which we answer many words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says the same thing as שמואל, to support his reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase תניא נמי הכי means an earlier תנאי source agrees with the אמורא. The ברייתא adds the word הרבה, 'many,' stressing that a lot of the הגדה is said over the מצה.

keyTerms.meaning: it was also taught this way (a ברייתא supports)

phrases.english: It was also taught so:
'Lechem oni'
is bread over which one answers many words.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports שמואל's reading in step 23.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא with the identical reading

steps.title: Another reading: the bread of a poor man
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives a second reading: עני is spelled without a ו, meaning 'poor,' so מצה is like a poor person's bread. A poor person usually eats a broken piece.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation: 'לחם עוני' — it is written 'עני' (poor). Just as a poor person usually eats a broken piece...
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא offers a second way to read the word, based on its spelling. The sentence continues on the next amud, so this step sets up a comparison that will be finished there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The written spelling עני, without a ו, means 'a poor person.' Since a poor person usually has only a piece of bread, not a whole loaf, the comparison will teach something about using a broken מצה at the סדר.
steps.confusionAlert: The word is read (pronounced) עוני but written עני without a ו. This second reading is built on the written spelling.

phrases.english: Another explanation:
'Lechem oni'
'oni' is written (without a vav, meaning 'poor'),
just as a poor person, whose way is with a broken piece,

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּבָר אַחֵר לֶחֶם עוֹנִי עֹנִי כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second reading of the same פסוק within the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Comparison begins: מצה is like a poor man's bread, which is usually a broken piece. The conclusion continues on the next amud.
